Senses.Explanation: The inner chamber is what lies past a house’s public gate and hall; Chan records bend that architectural depth into the inner matter of the named teaching figure’s house, lineage formulations, or an encounter. An interlocutor asks whether two establishments differ in “public frontage and inner chamber,” making the outer/inner house contrast explicit. Wanan Daoyan says only one who enters the gateless gate can sit within the inner chamber. Sanfeng Hanyue Fazang calls Linji’s mysteries, essentials, guest, and host the inner matters differentiated within one phrase. Baiyu Jingsi says not to seek the inner chamber elsewhere; an unnamed monk says Zhaozhou’s walls admitted him and asks about the inner-chamber matter; Yingning Jing directs one who wants to enter deeply to inquire of an elder. The Zen bend preserves the spatial constraint—past frontage into the inside—while applying it to what is intimate or internal to a teaching house, without inventing a secret teaching formulation.

Senses.Explanation: The head-of-hall reverend is the monastery’s presiding abbot or teacher as named from the community’s institutional side. Pure rules put the title into invitations, announcements, and appointments: a formal notice invites a head-of-hall reverend, a hall attendant announces that he has cancelled evening interview, and a rector cites his instruction when appointing an officer. Reception language asks the head-of-hall reverend at Wuzu to expound before the assembly. Tianyi Yihuai credits such the named teaching figure with close formation and encouragement, while Hongjue Min uses the title when announcing the death of the present monastery’s presiding teacher. The Chan bend is institutional rather than symbolic: the named teaching figure of public encounter is named here as the person who presides over the hall and whose word organizes its communal offices and events.

Senses.Explanation: The true eye at the crown is an emphatic image for the capacity to discern and respond without being trapped by the presented terms. Yongzhang Jun and Fuxin Bencai say that it must be opened or that everyone has it; a preface praises Hanxiu Ruqian as possessing it; other records test it in questions about light and the teaching seat. Zen relocates “seeing” to the crown of the head to mark an examiner’s decisive vision, not an anatomical organ.
